FOREWORD
As the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Timor-Leste, I am honoured to present the United Nations
Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2026–2030. This document constitutes our
principal strategic instrument for supporting national development priorities and accelerating progress
toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
This Cooperation Framework is the product of deep and inclusive consultation with the Government of TimorLeste, development partners, civil society and communities across the country. It builds on the lessons of
the past cycle and reflects a renewed ambition to leave no one behind.
Anchored in the Timor-Leste Strategic Development Plan (2011–2030), Timor-Leste’s accession to ASEAN
and its roadmap and informed by the Common Country Analysis (CCA), the UNSDCF supports the country’s
aspirations for inclusive economic transformation, including as a potential competitive ASEAN country,
resilient and equitable service delivery, sustainable use of natural resources and transparent, accountable
governance.
As a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) and Least Developed Country (LDC), Timor-Leste faces heightened
climate and economic vulnerabilities; the UNSDCF addresses these challenges by integrating gender equality,
youth empowerment, climate resilience and human rights as cross-cutting priorities and aligned to the Doha
Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries for the Decade 2022-2031 (DPoA).
The UN Country Team in Timor-Leste stands ready to support government in the delivery of the commitment
of the UNSDCF 2026-2030 through coherent and coordinated support, partnerships, digital innovation and
leveraging the full breadth of the UN’s global knowledge and local presence. On behalf of the UN Country
Team in Timor-Leste, I would like to once again thank the government of Timor-Leste and all other partners,
for their trust and collaboration and look forward to our continued joint efforts to build a more inclusive,
peaceful and sustainable future for all in Timor-Leste.
Funmi Balogun
Resident Coordinator

JOINT STATEMENT
In its resolution 72/279 of 31 May 2018, the United Nations General Assembly created a dedicated, impartial,
independent, empowered and sustainable development-focused coordination function for the United Nations
Development System (UNDS). The United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework
(UNSDCF) 2026–2030 is in line with Member States’ call for a United Nations development system reform
to boost coordination in supporting countries to achieve the Agenda 2030.
The UNSDCF is aligned with the national vision set out in the Strategic Development Plan 2011–2030, the
Programme of the IX Constitutional Government and sectoral strategies. It reflects our shared priorities for
advancing social capital and inclusive services, sustainable economic transformation, resilient infrastructure
and environmental stewardship and democratic governance and institutional effectiveness.
The UNSDCF is grounded in the principles of national ownership, mutual accountability, human rights, gender
equality and the commitment to Leave No One Behind (LNOB). It also emphasizes the need for transformative
partnerships, investment in human capital and a multi-sectoral approach that integrates climate resilience,
youth engagement and digital innovation.
We acknowledge the critical role ofthe UNSDCF in supporting Timor-Leste’s global and regional commitments,
including SDG implementation, accession to ASEAN, WTO and integration into the global economy. This
joint commitment reflects our determination to achieve sustainable development outcomes that improve
the lives of all people in Timor-Leste.
Together, we reaffirm our resolve to implement this Cooperation Framework with urgency, transparency and
solidarity. In signing, the partners endorse this UNSDCF and emphasize their joint commitment towards
fulfilling its objectives.
Bendito dos Santos Freitas
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation

The United Nations Sustainable Development
Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2026–2030 is the
primaryinstrumentguidingthecollectivecontributions
of the UN development system in Timor-Leste. It
represents a strategic partnership between theUnited
Nations and the Government of Timor-Leste, aligned
with the country’s StrategicDevelopmentPlan (2011–
2030)

and Timor-Leste’s commitments to the 2030 Agenda
for Sustainable Development. It reflects the shared
vision for a more inclusive, resilient and sustainable
Timor-Leste, particularly considering the country’s
status as both a Least Developed Country (LDC) and
a Small Island Developing State (SIDS), with unique
structural and environmental vulnerabilities.
TheUNSDCF is the result of an inclusive, participatory
process co-led with the Government and involving
civil society, private sector, youth, development
partners and communities across the country.
Key partners included particularly women’s
groups, youth-led organizations, organizations of
persons with disabilities (OPDs) and private sector
actors. Additionally, development partners and
the government were consulted through bilateral
engagements and the UN-Government Steering
Committee.
The overarching Strategic Vision guiding this
Cooperation Framework is that:
“
By 2030, the people of Timor-Leste,
particularly women, children, youth,
people with disabilities and the most
vulnerable, thrive in dignity through
equitable access to quality services
and decent work in a diversified and
sustainable economy. This progress
is supported by resilient governance
systems, strengthened capacities for
disaster risk reduction and climate
adaptation and a commitment to
environmental sustainability.”

Change and operationalized through specific focus

The Cooperation Framework pays particular attention
to advancing human rights, gender equality, disability
inclusion, youth engagement and the Leave No One
Behind principles. These cross-cutting commitments
guide all interventions and are embedded within both
the results and accountability frameworks.

CHAPTER 1: COUNTRY CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT VISION
1.1 Country Context and
Development Landscape
Since the restoration of independence, TimorLeste has made steady progress in state-building,
peace consolidation and service delivery. However,
development gains remain fragile and uneven. High
poverty and inequality persist, with women, youth,
persons with disabilities and rural communities at
heightened risk of being left behind. Challenges
include limited economic diversification, climate
vulnerability and institutional capacity gaps. This
Cooperation Framework is grounded in the Strategic
Development Plan (2011–2030), the Programme
of the IX Constitutional Government and the 2030
Agenda. It reflects a shared commitment to building
an inclusive, resilient and prosperous Timor-Leste.
1.2 Social Capital and Inclusion
Over 60% of Timor-Leste’s population is under 25,
presenting the promise of a demographic opportunity
butalsochallengesonservicedelivery.Whileaccessto
education, health and social protection has improved,
disparities in quality and reach persist, particularly
once age, gender, disabilities and geographies
(urban/rural) are considered. Learning outcomes
remain low; dropout rates are high among girls and
children with disabilities. The health system faces
persistent barriers, including workforce shortages
and gaps in maternal and child health. Malnutrition is
critical: 47% of children under five are stunted. Social
protection has expanded but remains fragmented.
Gender inequality remains a major constraint:
women face barriers in education, health, economic
participation and safety, with gender-based violence
widespread. Youth face high unemployment, limited
skills development opportunities and marginalization
from civic processes. Addressing these barriers is
essential to unlocking the full human potential of
the country.
1.3 Economic Transformation
Timor-Leste’s economy remains heavily dependent
on petroleum revenues, an unsustainable model
given resource depletion and market volatility.
The non-oil economy—centred on subsistence
agriculture and informal labour—lacks productivity
and resilience. Rural livelihoods are constrained
by climate variability, low market integration and
limited investment. Women and youth face additional
obstacles in accessing land, finance and innovation.
The private sector is small, with access to finance,
regulatory complexity and skills deficits posing major
barriers. Opportunities exist to expand MSMEs,
particularly those led by youth and women and to
leverage digital innovation. Accession to ASEAN
and the WTO presents opportunities for structural
reform and market integration. ASEAN accession
in particular requires Timor-Leste to demonstrate
progress in economic diversification, infrastructure
and workforce skills development, while WTO
membership demands alignment with trade and
regulatory standards.
These regional and global integration processes
are not only milestones but also drivers of reform,
providing incentives for Timor-Leste to accelerate
private sector growth, improve competitiveness and
strengthen governance systems. Diversification
will also lean on a Blue Economy transition that
modernizes small-scale fisheries and coastal value
chains, improves port / market access and embeds
environmental safeguards in marine-based tourism
and aquaculture.
1.4 Climate Change and Resilience
As both an LDC and SIDS, Timor-Leste is highly
exposed to natural hazards—floods, landslides,
droughts and cyclones—which are intensifying due
to climate change. Climate risks affect agriculture,
infrastructure, water, health and food security.
Environmental degradation further undermines
resilience, with women and rural communities
especially vulnerable. National commitments such
as the NDC and National Adaptation Plan signal
strong policy intent. However, implementation is
constrained by limited capacity, financing and data.
The Cooperation Framework supports integrated
climate action—advancing nature-based solutions,
early warning systems and climate-smart agriculture
and infrastructure—to strengthen systemic resilience.
The Blue Economy lens strengthens adaptation
by aligning coastal planning, reef and mangrove
restoration and risk-informed fisheries management
with resilient livelihoods for coastal communities.UNSDCF TIMOR-LESTE 2026 - 2030 | 17

CHAPTER 1: COUNTRY CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT VISION
1.5 Governance and Institutions
Timor-Leste has maintained peace and democratic
stability since independence, holding regular
elections and nurturing a dynamic civil society. Yet,
institutional capacity for service delivery remains
limited, especially at the municipal level. Access to
justice is uneven, particularly for women, persons
with disabilities and rural populations. Public finance
systems are under reform but require enhanced
transparency and responsiveness. Decentralization
is a national priority to improve inclusive governance
and local service delivery. Young people remain
underrepresented in civic life and decision-making.
Strengthening governance requires advancing human
rights, inclusive participation, subnational capacity
and digitaltransformation. Full membership inASEAN
and the WTO will require stronger bureaucratic and
institutional capacities to meet regional obligations,
harmonize laws and standards and ensure TimorLeste’s effective participation in intergovernmental
processes. The UNSDCF will support these
institutionalreforms, anchoring them in human rights,
inclusion and transparency.
1.6 Cross-Cutting Themes and
Integrated Approach
The Cooperation Framework adopts a rights-based
and intersectional approach to development,
with gender equality, youth empowerment and
climate resilience as core cross-cutting themes.
These dimensions intersect to create overlapping
vulnerabilities—particularly for rural women, young
people and persons with disabilities. As an LDC and
SIDS, Timor-Leste’s exposure to climate risk is an
existential challenge. The Cooperation Framework
embeds climate resilience and social inclusion
across all outcomes, supporting gender-responsive
education, youth-driven innovation, climate-smart
agriculture and resilient infrastructure. Entry points
within each outcome area are leveraged to address
root causes of exclusion and build pathways for
equitable development. These cross-cutting priorities
also intersect with Timor-Leste’s path to ASEAN and
WTO membership, where inclusive social policies,
climate resilience and youth empowerment are
increasingly central to regional and global agendas.
Finally, as an integrative theme for SIDS, the Blue
Economy will be used to link gender-responsive
and youth-responsive livelihood opportunities with
climate resilience in coastal municipalities.
1.7 Risk Landscape and UN
Response
Timor-Leste’s development trajectory is shaped by
interlinked risks, including economic dependency,
climate-related shocks, political transitions and
institutional capacity constraints. These risks have
the potential to disrupt progress toward sustainable
and inclusive developmentif not proactivelymanaged.
The United Nations system will apply an integrated
and forward-looking approach to risk mitigation.
This includes scenario planning, early warning
systems and adaptive programming that enable
timely responses to emerging risks. Crisis prevention,
conflict sensitivity, human rights and resiliencebuilding will be embedded across all Cooperation
Frameworkoutcomes andimplementationmodalities.
The UN will work with national partners to strengthen
disaster risk management, promote economic
diversification and improve governance systems
to ensure transparency and accountability. Efforts
will also focus on addressing social inequalities
and protecting the rights of marginalized groups,
including women, youth, people with disabilities
and rural communities. Risk monitoring will be
integrated into the Cooperation Framework’s
Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning and Data (MELD)
system, allowing for continuous assessment and
adjustment through Joint Steering Committee
reviews and annual work planning processes.
Risks also arise from the demands of ASEAN and
WTO accession, where challenges to implement
agreed reforms could undermine credibility and slow
integration. TheUNSDCF embeds risk monitoring and
scenario planning to ensure that accession-related
commitments are metin ways that protect vulnerable
populations and strengthen resilience.C3. HAPTER 2: OUTCOMES,

CHAPTER 2: OUTCOMES, PRIORITIES AND PATHWAYS
The United Nations Sustainable Development
Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2026–2030 is
the primary strategic tool for UN system support
to Timor-Leste. It is fully aligned with the country’s
Strategic Development Plan (SDP) 2011–2030 and
the IX Constitutional Government Programme. It is
also informed by national monitoring institutions,
including the National Institute of Statistics (INETL)
and the newly established Performance Monitoring
& Evaluation Unit (UMAD) in the Ministry of Finance.
The Cooperation Framework is grounded in the
principles of country leadership, ownership and the
use of national systems - as used by the Government
of Timor-Leste: "country-led, country-owned and
through country systems". These reflect TimorLeste’s vision of sovereign, effective development
partnerships. In line with guidance from the Ministry
of Finance, the UN will ensure full alignment with
national priorities, including active participation in
structured reporting and policy dialogue mechanisms.
The Cooperation Framework is organized around
four interlinked Strategic Priorities that mirror the
SDP pillars: Social Capital and Inclusive Services,
Economic Development, Disaster and Climate
Resilience and Resilient Infrastructure and
Democratic Governance. These were identified
through a participatory process involving national
institutions, civil society, development partners and
the UN system. They reflect both the country’s longterm aspirations and a shift toward a more equitable
and resilient development model. Each Strategic
Priority is supported by specific Focus Areas, based
on theUN’s comparative advantage, lessons frompast
frameworks and alignment with national strategies
and the Common Country Analysis. Together, they
form a unified platform for impactful, results-based
support.
The Cooperation Framework aims to catalyse
systemic change, promote rights-based development
and ensure inclusion for all, especially those left
furthest behind. As a Small Island Developing State
and Least Developed Country, Timor-Leste faces
persistent vulnerabilities that require strengthened
resilience, environmental sustainability and robust
institutional capacity. The Cooperation Framework
acknowledges these challenges while reinforcing
Timor-Leste’s ambitions for ASEAN and WTO
accession. These priorities are addressed through
work on governance, economic diversification and
human capital development.
TheUN will supportthese efforts through coordinated
mechanisms that build on its system-wide
comparative advantage. This includes regulatory
alignment, institutional strengthening and regional
collaboration.Recent engagement with ASEAN opens
a pathway for a more integrated approach, enabling
the UN to accompany Timor-Leste in its global and
regional integration.
2.1 UN Comparative Advantage
The UN system in Timor-Leste brings diverse
mandates, technical expertise and long-standing
partnership. Its strength lies in coordinated, crosssectoral approaches that promote coherence across
national priorities. The UN provides integrated policy
advice, capacity development and strategic support
for inclusive service delivery and governance. A core
strength is its role in advancing evidence-based
decision-making, especially through its work with
line ministries on planning, monitoring and public
finance. The UN will continue to support national
statistical systems, data platforms and results-based
budgeting to institutionalize inclusive and transparent
governance.
The UN serves as a neutral platform for convening
diverse actors across sectors and levels. It also
brings access to regional expertise and SouthSouth cooperation, enabling exchange with ASEAN
countries and others facing similar development
challenges. The UNSDCF also complements TimorLeste’s regional and global integration trajectory,
particularly ASEAN and WTO accession. The UN
brings comparative advantage in helping the country
align national systems with ASEAN frameworks.
Beyond accession, the UN will support TimorLeste to sustain compliance with ASEAN and WTO
obligations, leveraging South-South cooperation
and regional expertise to embed reforms and ensure
that integration delivers tangible benefits to all

The United Nations System will support
national priorities by providing integrated
policy advice, strengthening systems and
capacities at all levels and building inclusive
partnerships. It will help expand access
to quality services, promote sustainable
livelihoods, strengthen resilience to climate
and disaster risks and improve governance
that is accountable and responsive.
Across all efforts, the United Nations will
prioritize gender equality, climate action
and reaching those furthest behind, drawing
on innovation, digital solutions and global
cooperation to advance human rights and
sustainable progress.
The UN system will use these platforms to scale
solutions, align development support with national
systems and mobilize innovative financing.
Volunteerism strengthens civic engagement,
social cohesion and community resilience. The
UN will promote volunteerism as a cross-cutting
implementation modality, supporting national and
local efforts through youth engagement, disaster
response and inclusive service delivery. In partnership
with national institutions and civil society, the UN
will help expand opportunities for volunteers—
especially young people and women—to contribute
to sustainable development and local ownership of
results.
This includes efforts to unlock non-earmarked
and pooled resources and to prioritize strategic
underfunded areas such as food systems, local
governanceandinteroperabledatasystems.Allefforts
will be framed by national priorities and integrated
into public systems to maximize sustainability and
impact.
2.2 Vision
By 2030, the people of Timor-Leste, particularly
women, children, youth, people with disabilities
and the most vulnerable, thrive in dignity through
equitable access to quality services and decent
work in a diversified and sustainable economy.
This progress is supported by resilient governance
systems, strengthened capacities for disaster risk
reduction and climate adaptation and a commitment
to environmental sustainability.
This Vision reflects Timor-Leste’s long-standing
development aspirations as outlined in the Strategic
Development Plan (2011–2030), structured around its
four pillars: Social Capital, Economic Development,
Infrastructure Development and Institutional
Framework. It also aligns with the IX Constitutional
Government Programme, including commitments
to deepen investment in social capital, modernize
infrastructure, strengthen governance and promote
inclusive economic transformation. The Vision
was shaped through consultations with national
stakeholders and reflects shared development
priorities. To track progress, the UNSDCF will use
jointly defined indicators and baselines aligned with
the SDP and SDGs. Results-based monitoring and
evaluation will be coordinated with INETL and UMAD,
ensuring national ownership and alignment with
performance management systems.
The Cooperation Framework’s four outcome areas
represent integrated pathways to address TimorLeste’s multidimensional development challenges.
By focusing on inclusive service delivery, sustainable
livelihoods, resilient infrastructure and accountable
governance, the UN system will support national
efforts to reduce poverty, inequality and vulnerability
to climate and economic shocks, contributing to

2.4 Outcome 1: Social Capital and
Inclusive Services
This outcome is rooted in Timor-Leste’s Strategic
Development Plan (2011–2030), which prioritizes
human capital as a foundation for national
development. It also reflects the IX Constitutional
Government’s focus on expanding equitable access
to quality public services, especially forthose furthest
behind. The United Nations will supportthis outcome
through coordinated policy advice, capacity building
and inclusive partnerships that uphold rights and
promote well-being. To strengthen access to essential
services, the UN will promote the use of digital tools
in health, education and social protection. Support
will emphasize inclusive and interoperable systems
that improve outreach to remote and vulnerable
populations, enhance service quality and build
resilience to future shocks.

1.1. Education systems and policies enhanced
to expand equitable access, quality and
relevance of lifelong learning, particularly
forwomen, children, youth andmarginalized
groups, through inclusive curricula,
teacher capacity building and community
engagement.
The United Nations will supportthe transformation of
Timor-Leste’s education system to be more inclusive,
equitable and resilient. Efforts will strengthen access
to quality learning for girls, children with disabilities,
rural learners and other marginalized groups. Support
will focus on curriculum reform that promotes peace
and intercultural education, foundational and digital
skills, green competencies and inclusive teaching
methods. Special emphasis will be placed on
expanding mothertongue and multilingual education
and preserving traditional knowledge and civic
values. Improving teacher availability and training is
central, including sign language, braille and inclusive
pedagogy. The United Nations will also support early
childhood education, school readiness and flexible
learning options for children who are out of school.
To enhance system resilience, investments willtarget
climate and disaster ready infrastructure, stronger
education information systems and integrated
monitoring. Cross-sector efforts with nutrition, health,
child protection and social protection will promote
holistic child development. Digital solutions and
cultural preservation will be used to enrich learning
and ensure inclusive, future ready education for all.

1.3. Improved access to quality nutrition
services andstrengthenedrelevant systems
to prevent malnutrition and improve diets.
The United Nations will support national efforts to
reduce malnutrition and strengthen food and nutrition
security. Focus will be on children, adolescents and
pregnant and lactating women, using a life course
and systems strengthening approach. UN support
will integrate preventive and curative nutrition
services into primary health care and community
platforms. Priority interventions include maternal
counselling, promotion of infant and young child
feeding, micronutrient supplementation, adolescent
nutrition and the treatment of acute malnutrition.
Positive nutrition practices will be promoted through
caregiver engagement, nurturing care and improved
school food environments. To build resilience, the
United Nations will support shock responsive and
nutrition sensitive systems, including school feeding
with local and fortified foods, dietary diversity and
food fortification policy. Social protection will
target young children and pregnant women at risk
of stunting. Support will strengthen coordination
across health, agriculture, education, WASH and
social protection. Investments in data and climate
preparedness will improve monitoring and enhance
nutrition outcomes over time.
1.4. Social Protection frameworks strengthened
and tailored to address vulnerabilities and
promote inclusion for women, children,
youth and the most marginalized
populations
The United Nations will support the expansion and
integration of inclusive, gender responsive, nutrition
sensitive and shock responsive systems. Efforts will
follow a life cycle approach, prioritizing children,
older persons, persons with disabilities, informal
workers and others facing overlapping vulnerabilities.
The UN will assist in strengthening policy and legal
frameworks for universal and contributory schemes
through fiscal analysis, evidence generation and
gender responsive planning and budgeting. Support
will include the development of digital systems for
beneficiary registries, targeting and payments to
improve programme efficiency and transparency.
Subnational capacities will be strengthened to
deliver social assistance and insurance, improve
linkages with health, education, WASH, nutrition and
employment and extend services to remote
communities. Social protection will be embedded in
disaster preparedness to enable continuity and rapid
scale up during crises. The UN will promote nutrition
focused support for pregnant and breastfeeding
women and children under two and expand cash
transfers that enhance women’s economic autonomy.
Inclusivecommunicationandcommunityengagement
will improve uptake and accountability. Integrated
systems will help reduce poverty, advance human
development and build resilience.UN plans to provide
basic comprehensive primary healthcare services to

2.8 Development Financing Context
for the Cooperation Framework
The UNSDCF 2026–2030 is being launched in the
context of an increasingly volatile and constrained
development financing landscape. Timor-Leste’s
public financing remains heavily reliant on a few core
sources—namely, the Petroleum Fund and Official
Development Assistance (ODA)—but both have been
subject to growing pressures.
Petroleum revenues continue to decline and fiscal
deficits continue to average 57–60% of non-oil
GDP. Domestic revenues reached $271 million in
2023, covering only 13% of total financing needs.
Remittances now represent the second-largest
external financial flow after petroleum revenues,
totalling $244.8 million in 2024—equivalent to nearly
9% of non-oil GDP. However, their contribution to
long-term development remains underleveraged.
Despite reforms in public financial management,
expenditure remains concentrated on recurrent
costs and subsidies, with limited space for capital
investments or expansion of social services.UNSDCF TIMOR-LESTE 2026 - 2030 | 51

country-led implementation, monitoring and
evaluation, with human rights, gender equality and

marginalized populations, including women, youth,
children and persons with disabilities. Institutional
capacity will be strengthened through inclusive,
climate-responsive and digitally enabled solutions
that build long-term resilience and social cohesion.

coordinated planning, shared monitoring frameworks
and alignment with national policies and the budget
